strengths: The paper proposes a training-free zero-shot anomaly generation framework, DeltaDeno, which addresses a practically important setting where real anomaly samples or task-specific fine-tuning are unavailable.

The delta-denoising attribution idea is technically sound: contrasting normal and anomaly prompt branches under a shared diffusion schedule yields an image-specific localization mask, and the use of normal-reference guided initialization, token-level prompt refinement, and spatial attention bias is well motivated and clearly described.

The experimental results on MVTec AD show consistent gains over the zero-shot baseline AnomalyAny on downstream detection metrics, and the ablation study verifies that the proposed modules (latent-mask inpainting, attention biasing, prompt refinement) each contribute to performance.

The paper is generally well written, positions the work clearly against few-shot and zero-shot anomaly generation methods, and provides a reasonable level of algorithmic detail and qualitative comparison.
The method is compatible with off-the-shelf diffusion and segmentation models, making it practical for rapid data bootstrapping and stress testing without anomaly labels.
weaknesses: The main quantitative evaluation is limited to MVTec AD; although the paper states that other datasets are in the appendix, the main manuscript does not provide cross-domain or multi-dataset evidence to substantiate the claimed cross-category generalization.

The generation-quality improvement over AnomalyAny is marginal on the reported IS and IC-LPIPS metrics (e.g., average IS 2.03 vs. 2.02), so the realism/diversity advantage is not strongly demonstrated by the main metrics.

Several important implementation details and hyperparameters are missing from the main paper, including the attention-bias strength beta, the prompt-refinement step size and balance parameters eta/lambda, the number of refinement iterations, and how the SAM foreground mask is selected, which limits reproducibility.

The delta-denoising localization mechanism itself is not directly ablated against attention-map-based localization or a DiffEdit-style masking baseline, and there is no sensitivity analysis for key thresholds and the choice of t_mid.

The method requires the user to specify an anomaly type and a description prompt, which makes the 'zero-shot' setting less automatic than the framing might suggest and limits applicability when defect type is unknown.
Some few-shot baselines still outperform the proposed method on certain metrics (e.g., pixel-level AP in Table 2), and the comparison to zero-shot methods is limited to a single recent baseline.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: zero-shot anomaly generation without any real anomalous samples, fine-tuning, or task-specific retraining, which directly tackles the scarcity issue that motivates the field.

The delta-denoising attribution idea (contrasting two synchronized diffusion branches under normal vs. anomaly prompts and accumulating per-step latent deltas into an image-specific mask) is conceptually clean, well-integrated with mask-guided latent inpainting, and yields sharper localization than attention-map heuristics used by prior ZSAG work.

Empirical results are consistent and fairly convincing: the method attains higher Inception Score and IC-LPIPS across most MVTec AD categories (Tab. 1) and yields clear downstream gains in image/pixel AUROC and AP when training a U-Net on synthesized data, especially against the main ZSAG baseline AnomalyAny (Tab. 2).

Ablation studies (Tab. 3, Figs. 4 and 5) isolate the contributions of latent-mask inpainting, spatial attention biasing, and token-level prompt refinement, and additionally demonstrate controllable defect morphology via the description prompt.
The paper is clearly written and organized, the pipeline is well illustrated (Fig. 2), the algorithm is spelled out (Alg. 1), and the code release is promised, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core mechanism (contrasting a source/normal branch against a target/anomaly branch to derive an edit mask under a shared schedule) is closely related to DiffEdit, which is cited but whose relationship to 'delta-denoising attribution' is not discussed in depth; the incremental novelty of the attribution scheme relative to this prior line is not fully articulated.

Evaluation in the main text is restricted to MVTec AD; claims of cross-category generalization would be substantially stronger with in-main-paper results on other benchmarks (e.g., VisA, MVTec LOCO, or the industrial categories shown in Fig. 3), rather than deferring them to the appendix.

Several hyperparameters appear hand-tuned (mask thresholds 0.6 and 0.35, partial-noise ratio γ=0.3, bias weight β, and the loss weights η and λ) without a sensitivity analysis, leaving the robustness of the method to these choices unclear.

Downstream detection is evaluated only with a simple U-Net trained on the synthesized data; it is not shown whether the generated anomalies remain beneficial for stronger or more modern detectors (e.g., PatchCore-style memory banks or transformer-based AD models).

The procedure for selecting the anomaly prompt and description prompt per category is under-specified; it is unclear how much manual effort or prior knowledge is needed to pick the 'minimal prompt pair' and descriptor, which matters for the claimed practical zero-shot setting.

The token-level prompt refinement (semantic distillation anchor plus context-alignment MSE) is described somewhat ad hoc; the motivation for the specific anchor construction and the effect of its quality on results are not thoroughly examined.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important setting: zero-shot anomaly generation without any real anomalous samples, masks, or fine-tuning, which is a genuine departure from the dominant few-shot fine-tuning paradigm.

The pipeline is clearly described and reproducible in outline: a two-branch prompt-contrast diffusion scheme, an accumulator over denoising steps, mask-guided latent inpainting, normal-reference guided initialization, and prompt/attention refinement, with an explicit algorithm box and stated hyperparameters (SD v1.5, T=100, gamma=0.3, thresholds 0.6/0.35).

Downstream anomaly-detection gains over the main zero-shot baseline (AnomalyAny) are consistent and non-trivial on MVTec AD (e.g., mean AUC_i 84.7 vs 77.6, AP_i 91.3 vs 87.1), and the ablation study (Table 3) shows each proposed module contributes monotonically.

The Anomaly Semantic Distillation result (Fig. 5) demonstrates a useful, qualitatively convincing form of controllability, letting description prompts steer defect type and severity while remaining training-free.

Qualitative comparison (Fig. 3) and cross-category results outside MVTec AD are provided, and the authors explicitly note the data-leakage issue in few-shot baselines, which is a fair and useful observation.
Limitations are discussed honestly (limited evaluation protocols, limited controllability, difficulty with abstract/logical defects).
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. The core mechanism, contrasting denoiser predictions under a shared schedule for a normal vs. anomalous prompt to derive an edit mask, is essentially the DiffEdit mask-estimation recipe (Couairon et al., cited as [9] and acknowledged in Sec. 2.1) transposed to anomaly generation. The additional ingredients (prompt refinement, attention biasing) closely resemble established prompt-to-prompt / Attend-and-Excite style manipulations, so the aggregate contribution reads as an engineering adaptation rather than a new principle.

The paper's central claimed advantage, precise image-specific localization, is not directly evaluated. Table 1 reports only IS and IC-LPIPS (generation quality/diversity), and Table 2 reports downstream detector metrics; there is no direct mask-quality evaluation (e.g., IoU/AP against ground-truth defect masks, or comparison to AnomalyAny's attention masks at the mask level). The 'strong localization fidelity' claim is therefore supported only indirectly.

Generation realism is assessed solely with Inception Score, which is known to be a weak and easily gamed proxy for photorealism in this setting, and no FID or human/MM-LLM evaluation is provided. The realism claims rest largely on a handful of qualitative examples.

The ZSAG comparison set is thin: essentially one zero-shot baseline (AnomalyAny), with all other methods being few-shot and relegated to 'reference' status. Given the fast-moving nature of zero-shot anomaly generation, a broader zero-shot comparison would be needed to establish state of the art.

The delta-denominating accumulator and thresholding scheme (Eqs. 8-10) is heuristic: there is no analysis of why per-step L2 differences isolate anomalies, why the mid-trajectory threshold is appropriate, or how sensitive the mask is to t_mid, tau_mid, and the prompt wording. Since both branches share the same normal-image initialization, it is also unclear how much the mask is genuinely image-specific versus prompt-driven.

Several claims are stated more strongly than the evidence supports (e.g., 'higher resolution boundaries,' 'precise masks,' 'photorealistic fidelity') without quantitative mask or fidelity metrics backing them, and no trivial ablation (e.g., inpainting with a SAM foreground mask but no delta attribution) is given to isolate the value of the delta mechanism itself.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: the description-prompt anchor e_detail and the prompt-refinement hyperparameters (lambda, eta, step size, iteration count) are not fully specified in the main text, and key results (other datasets) are deferred to an unavailable appendix.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely well-motivated problem: existing anomaly generation pipelines (FSAG) require scarce real anomalous samples, which contradicts the motivation for generation. DeltaDeno is fully training-free and requires no anomalous pixels, making the setting meaningful for industrial deployment.

The core mechanism (delta-denoising attribution) is technically coherent and clearly described: two synchronized diffusion branches driven by a minimal normal/anomaly prompt pair, per-step latent deltas accumulated into an image-specific localization map, then used as a latent inpainting mask during late denoising. The pipeline is well laid out in Fig. 2, Algorithm 1, and the equations (7)–(11), and the components fit together logically.

Strong and consistent empirical results. On MVTeC AD, DeltaDeno achieves mean AUCi 84.7 / APi 91.3 (SD1.5) and 89.7 / 94.8 (FLUX), outperforming AnomalyAny (77.6 / 87.3) and AnoStyler (84.4 / 91.5) under the same one-shot ZSAG protocol. Similar gains on VisA (mean AUCi 85.1 with FLUX vs 74.7 / 76.5). The cross-backbone transfer from SD1.5 to FLUX-1.dev without architecture-specific tuning supports the model-agnostic claim.

Ablations are reasonably thorough: module ablation on latent-mask inpainting, attention biasing, and prompt refinement (Table 4); threshold sensitivity (Fig. 5, Table 6); SAM dependence (Sec. C.2); and runtime/memory (Sec. C.3, 10.25 s/img and 10.36 GiB vs AnomalyAny's 67.4 s and 31.7 GiB). The comparison against FSAG methods (Table 5) is informative even though the advantage is one-sided.

The discussion in Appendix D on the shortcomings of existing evaluation protocols for ZSAG (IC-LPIPS anchoring on real anomalies, entanglement of generator quality with detector choice, absence of mask-quality metrics) is a thoughtful and useful contribution that most papers in this area omit.

Reproducibility is largely adequate: backbone, denoising steps, γ, thresholds, β, λ, and step size η are all specified in Sec. 4.1 and Appendix B, and the method builds on standard public components (SD1.5, SAM, FLUX).

Limitations are explicitly acknowledged (evaluation protocols, limited controllability of semantic distillation, difficulty with abstract/logical defects), and an Internet-collected ceramic bottle example (Fig. 3, last row) partially supports the cross-category generalization claim.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. The central delta-denoising attribution is very close to DiffEdit-style prompt-contrast masking, which the paper itself acknowledges in Sec. 2.1 ("DiffEdit derives an edit mask by contrasting source and target prompts under a shared schedule"). The delta is the synchronized dual-branch formulation, the accumulator S, and the reuse of the mask for late-stage inpainting. Prompt refinement and attention biasing are useful but engineering-level additions; the aggregate technical advance over existing prompt-contrast editing is incremental.

Mask quality — one of the paper's two headline claims ("precise masks", Fig. 1) — is never quantitatively evaluated. There is no metric aligning generated masks with generated defects (e.g., IoU against ground-truth defect regions on MVTeC, or a paired mask-image consistency score). The paper acknowledges this gap in Appendix D.3 but does not close it, and downstream AUCp/APp conflate mask accuracy with detector quality. This is a substantive gap given the claim.

The method requires the user to specify {anomaly type} in the prompt (e.g., crack, hole, scratch), and the ZSAG claim of "no task-specific re-training" is therefore somewhat softened: the method does require task-relevant semantic priors in text form. The paper argues that generic terms (damage, defect) suffice, but no systematic evaluation of how sensitive the pipeline is to the anomaly-type token is provided beyond the description-prompt ablation in Fig. 6.

No variance or error bars are reported for any table. Given that downstream U-Net training on synthetic data is a stochastic process, single-run numbers (Tables 1–6) are insufficient to judge whether the reported gaps (e.g., 84.7 vs 84.4 vs 77.6) are significant. At minimum, multi-seed standard deviations for the downstream detection tables would strengthen the claims.

Comparison set for generation quality (Table 1) is narrow and IS is a weak metric for industrial defect realism. DRAEM and Cut-Paste appear only qualitatively (Fig. 3), and several recent ZSAG/FSAG baselines (e.g., DefectFill, SEA S) are omitted. Also, IS and IC-LPIPS are used despite the paper's own Appendix D critique that these metrics are misaligned with ZSAG — this is not fatal, but the inconsistency is not addressed.

The FLUX-based results (Tables 2, 3, 5) are reported without any description of how the pipeline was adapted (30 steps, guidance 3.5, strength 0.8 are only in Appendix B.1). Since FLUX is a rectified-flow model rather than a DDIM-style scheduler, the claim of "seamless transition" deserves more methodological explanation (e.g., how the accumulator and mid-step mask are defined under flow matching).

The SAM-derived foreground prior (M_fg) is a non-trivial external dependency. The ablation shows a drop to 83.3/90.7/82.1/29.2 without it, which is modest, but the mechanism by which M_fg biases cross-attention for the anomaly token only is under-explained, and the interplay between M_fg (early) and M_mid (late) in Eq. (13) is not analyzed in isolation.

No quantitative evaluation of cross-category generalization is given; Fig. 3 last row is a single example. The paper's third contribution ("cross-category generalization across industrial and other domains") is thus only weakly supported.

Some statements need tightening: "training-free" coexists with a gradient-based prompt-refinement loop (Eq. 12) that optimizes text embeddings, and the paper does not report the cost of this loop separately. Also, the phrase "preserve the surrounding context" would benefit from a quantitative reconstruction/background-fidelity metric (e.g., LPIPS on the unmasked region).

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem: zero-shot, training-free anomaly generation, avoiding the dependence of few-shot anomaly generation on scarce real anomalous samples and masks.

The proposed DeltaDeno framework is novel and technically sound: it contrasts two synchronized diffusion branches driven by normal and anomalous prompts, accumulates per-step denoising deltas to localize defects, and uses mask-guided latent inpainting with normal-reference initialization, token-level prompt refinement, and spatial attention biasing.
The method is clearly described with equations, an inference algorithm, and implementation details; the paper is generally well written and reproducible, with code promised.

Empirical evaluation is reasonably comprehensive, covering MVTec AD and VisA, generation quality (IS, IC-LPIPS), downstream anomaly detection, module ablations, threshold sensitivity, SAM dependence, runtime/memory analysis, and qualitative visualizations.

Results are strong for a zero-shot method: DeltaDeno achieves higher average IS and IC-LPIPS than prior ZSAG methods and yields competitive or superior downstream detection performance, sometimes approaching FSAG baselines despite using no real anomalous samples.
The paper includes an honest discussion of limitations and evaluation-protocol issues for ZSAG, which strengthens the scientific framing.
weaknesses: Mask quality is not evaluated quantitatively, even though anomaly generation is inherently a paired image-mask task. The paper acknowledges this in the appendix but still relies mainly on image-level metrics and downstream detection, which entangle mask accuracy with detector design.

The method requires an explicit anomaly-type prompt (e.g., crack, hole, scratch) and category name; although template-based, real zero-shot deployment may still depend on prompt vocabulary and severity descriptors, and the paper does not fully quantify sensitivity to prompt choice.

The framework depends on external pretrained models (Stable Diffusion, SAM, optionally FLUX) and test-time prompt-embedding optimization. It is training-free, but the computational/dependency cost is non-trivial, and the SAM-free ablation shows a noticeable performance drop.

Comparisons with FSAG methods are not apples-to-apples because FSAG methods use real anomalous samples and masks; the paper acknowledges this, but claims of competitiveness should be interpreted with that caveat in mind.

The generated anomalies are mostly structural or surface-level defects, while abstract/logical defects and fine-grained controllability remain limited; these limitations are acknowledged but still reduce the scope of the contribution.

Some hyperparameters (e.g., mask thresholds 0.6/0.35, partial-noise ratio 0.3) are fixed across categories, and while threshold analysis suggests reasonable robustness, broader cross-category and cross-dataset sensitivity is not fully explored.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and well-motivated problem: zero-shot anomaly generation (ZSAG) without any anomalous samples or model fine-tuning, which is practically relevant for industrial inspection where defects are scarce.

The pipeline is clean, clearly presented, and largely reproducible: prompt templates, hyperparameters (T=100, γ=0.3, β=4, λ=0.5, η=4, thresholds 0.6/0.35), and the inference algorithm (Alg. 1) are specified, and the method is shown to work on both SD1.5 and FLUX backbones.

Downstream detection gains over the direct ZSAG baseline AnomalyAny are non-trivial and consistent (Table 2 MVTec: mean AUC_i 84.7 vs 77.6; AUC_p 84.9 vs 83.3; Table 3 VisA: AUC_i 82.1 vs 74.7), and the efficiency advantage is meaningful (10.25 s/img, 10.36 GiB vs AnomalyAny's 67.4 s/img, 31.7 GiB), making the method practically usable.

The ablation study is reasonably thorough: module ablations (Table 4), threshold sensitivity (Table 6), SAM dependence (App. C.2), and description-prompt steering (Fig. 6) all support the design choices, and the qualitative visualizations (Figs. 3, 7, 8) are informative.

The manuscript is self-aware about evaluation weaknesses: App. D candidly discusses the limitations of IS/IC-LPIPS, of downstream detector entanglement, and of ignoring mask quality, and the Limitations section is honest. This strengthens the scientific case even where it does not resolve the concerns.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The central 'delta-denoising attribution' mechanism — contrasting denoiser predictions from two prompt-driven branches under a shared schedule to derive a mask — is essentially the DiffEdit idea (Couairon et al., cited as [9]), which the paper itself describes as 'deriv[ing] an edit mask by contrasting source and target prompts under a shared schedule.' The remaining components are also standard: normal-reference guided initialization is SDEdit-style partial noising; the late-stage blending in Eq. (11) is blended latent diffusion; the attention bias resembles Attend-and-Excite/Prompt-to-Prompt style control. The contribution is largely a recombination of existing techniques applied to a new domain.

Generation-quality gains are marginal and do not support the strong claims. In Table 1 the average IS is 2.05 vs AnoStyler 2.04 and AnomalyAny 2.02, and IC-LPIPS is 0.36 vs 0.32/0.33 — differences well within plausible run-to-run variance, yet the abstract claims 'great generation, realism.' No variance/confidence intervals or significance testing are reported for any metric.

The downstream detection evidence against the strongest baseline is mixed, undercutting the 'consistent gains' claim. On MVTec (Table 2), DeltaDeno(SD1.5) is essentially tied with AnoStyler on AP_i (91.3 vs 91.5) and AP_p (30.5 vs 30.2) and only clearly better on AUC_p; on VisA (Table 3) AP_p is substantially worse than AnoStyler (11.6 vs 16.6). The narrative emphasizes the comparison against the weaker AnomalyAny while the strongest ZSAG baseline is barely matched in several columns.

Mask quality — a headline claim ('precise masks') — is never evaluated against ground-truth defect masks. Masks are produced at a 64×64 latent resolution (Sec. B.1), which is coarse for pixel-accurate defect localization, and no IoU/pro-style metric, boundary accuracy, or mask-recall measure is provided. App. D.3 explicitly acknowledges this gap but does not fill it, so the precision claim rests on visual inspection and indirect downstream AUC_p/AP_p.

Evaluation scope and protocol are narrow for the generality claims. Only two (both industrial) datasets are used for the main comparison; the 'cross-category generalization' claim would be better supported by additional domains. The one-shot, 100-images-per-category, single-normal-image protocol yields small per-category samples, and the head-to-head against FSAG in Table 5 is confounded by the fact that FSAG methods see real anomalous samples (a point the authors acknowledge but still use to claim 'rivaling' FSAG).

Some framing is imprecise. The method is described as 'training-free,' but it performs per-sample gradient optimization of the anomaly-token embedding (Eq. 12, L_prompt) at inference, i.e., a test-time optimization. Hyperparameters β, η, and λ are fixed by hand and never ablated, and the authors concede the optimal mask thresholds vary by category (Sec. C.4), suggesting limited robustness across domains. No comparison is provided against a plain DiffEdit-style delta-attribution baseline (without prompt refinement, attention biasing, and inpainted warm-start) to isolate the value of the proposed additions beyond the qualitative Fig. 1.
